Latest Posts

  • Four nights, then two hours

    Nov 11, 2026

    Swami Sivasubramanian handed Kiro the rebuild of a replication engine that took him and Al Vermeulen four months twenty years ago, and supervised the agent for four nights before spotting the real problem: it had no way to check its results. Given a spec and a test environment, the rebuild took about two hours. AWS Emulator ships with agents writing all of its code and its tests corrected against real AWS first, an NBER study of 500,000 developers prices the same shape (+240% commits attenuating to +30% releases), and Microsoft FORGE Lab shows the security-side funnel: 26,502 scan findings became 59 upstream reports in four person-months.

  • The engine knew the row numbers

    Nov 10, 2026

    An agent-built, formally verified database engine reported 22-61x over DuckDB and Umbra for its query templates, and a sharper thing hid inside the plain-storage numbers: the synthesized code encodes how TPC-H's dbgen numbers its rows, so a join becomes pointer arithmetic, checked and correct on every database, fast on TPC-H's own generator. The TPC split TPC-D for this same disease in 1999. The durable fix is protocol, not proof: freeze the artifact, attack it with workloads it never saw, quote that number.

  • What silence permits

    Nov 3, 2026

    Unattended agent runtimes all end up answering one question: when the agent reaches for something irreversible and nobody answers, what happens. The past two weeks answered it from several directions — vincent 0.12's grants, Octomind's exit 75, ARTEX's mixed defaults (its delegated ask permits on silence), GitBook's Monday-evening intruders — and four questions that audit any runtime's consent surface in an afternoon.

  • Nov 12, 2026

    Nine build pipelines end their builds the same way: grep the binaries for the build machine’s path, and call the package clean when nothing comes back. RPM’s check-buildroot does it, Homebrew’s bottle scan does it, conda-build, Yocto, Arch’s makepkg, pkgsrc, FreeBSD’s stage QA, rattler-build and Julia’s BinaryBuilder all do a version of it. Every one of them rests on the same assumption, that a string constant in your source ends up in the binary as a string.

    GCC stopped keeping that promise. A string constant that gets copied into a buffer, through std::string construction, strcpy or memcpy, is stored as vector-width pieces instead; GCC has done this for strings up to 256 bytes since version 10, and since version 12 the limit scales with the target’s vector width, 512 bytes at AVX2, 1024 at AVX-512. I tried it on this machine’s GCC 15.2: std::string prefix = "/home/builder/rpmbuild/BUILD/tree-2.1.0"; at -O2. The program prints its path fine. Grep the binary for the path and you get zero. Two 16-byte constants happen to sit next to each other in .rodata, so strings shows /home/builder/rpmbuild/BUILD/tre, a path that exists nowhere, cut off mid-word, and the last eight bytes never reach .rodata at all: they ride through the copy inside a movabs immediate in the instruction stream. The post that documents this has a better punchline, a Homebrew prefix that greps back as /home/linuxbrew/xbrew/.linuxbrew, a directory nobody ever built in.

    What makes it treacherous rather than merely broken is that it depends on how each line uses the string. The same path passed only as a pointer, fopen(PREFIX "/x", "r"), stays in one piece, and my fopen-only binary greps 1 hit at the same -O2. One binary can carry the path both ways, and an auditor cannot tell from the outside which lines the compiler split. The speedup is hard to find, too: Clang emits the same vector stores from the intact string, and the split can cost more bytes than the string it replaces once the pieces are aligned. It clearly pays only when many strings share a long prefix and the pieces deduplicate.

    The mitigations are thin. -Os is the only full opt-out; my -Os binary greps 1 hit. -mstore-max=128 only rolls the behavior back to the pre-GCC-12 defaults, where strings up to 256 bytes still get split, and mine greps 0 with it. An opt-out flag is proposed on gcc-patches but has not landed. Conda and Spack take a second hit, because their install-time prefix rewriting patches the path in place, sed-style, which needs the path stored in one piece to work at all. The representation-independent route is to assert that the package rebuilds bit-for-bit elsewhere, but Debian’s comparison keeps the build directory fixed between its two builds (the .buildinfo file records it and the rebuild reuses it), so an embedded build path compares identical and goes unnoticed there too. To catch a path leak, the rebuild has to vary the path itself.

    If reproducible builds are not on your menu this quarter, there is a cheap heuristic, and I checked it: grep for a head window of the path instead of the whole path. In every binary I compiled, the first vector piece carried the path’s first 16 bytes, so a 15-byte prefix of the build root caught what the full-path grep called clean. It is a heuristic, not a guarantee, because the compiler owes the head piece nothing either; short strings can ride as scalar stores and even the head can split. Which is the same lesson from the other side: a build audit deserves one test it has probably never had, a binary you know is dirty pushed through to see whether the check can fail at all. On this compiler, the reassuring empty result has two meanings, and only one of them is clean.

  • Nov 12, 2026

    Deno is winding down. The team joined Cloudflare in October, and the runtime gets about a year of monthly bugfix and security releases before development ends. If you ever ran JavaScript you didn’t write inside deno run — YouTube’s player code, if you’re yt-dlp, or the blob a model just handed back, if you build agents — that cage has a closing date. The obvious new address is node --permission: grant nothing, the runtime refuses. yt-dlp already ships that path, per the launch code Yoonsoo Park quotes. On paper it reads like the same lease.

    Park measured the swap in October: thirteen probes, each a small attempt to reach outside the cage, run under Deno 2.9.7 and Node 22, 24 and 26. On the Node 22 LTS line, five of Deno’s twelve walls survive. I wanted that answer from my own machine, so I rebuilt his probe set against this host’s Node 22.23.2, one patch behind his, and ran it three times: a child with no grants, a fake secret in its environment, a work folder with a SQLite database and a secret file outside it, a symlink inside pointing out, a file handle handed in already open, two sibling Node processes running with no restrictions, a local HTTP server, and a plain-node control pass so a broken probe could not pass itself off as a blocked one.

    The matrix didn’t move. Five probes came back blocked: reading or writing files without a grant, and spawning /bin/echo. Eight got through. The child read its fake secret out of process.env, fetched the local server over HTTP and again over a raw TCP socket, and opened the outside database with node:sqlite and read the seeded row. The insert I did not take its word for; the parent counted two rows afterwards. The child read the inherited handle’s contents off a descriptor that never passed a permission check. And it switched on the inspector of both sibling processes, once through process._debugProcess(pid) and once with a plain SIGUSR1, each verified by that sibling’s own stderr printing Debugger listening.

    Granting read and write on the work folder changed exactly the two cells you would expect, and surfaced the hole Park also found: a symlink inside the allowed folder reads a file outside it. A folder grant is only as tight as the links inside it.

    Node is not surprised, and the docs say so in nearly these words: the model “implements a ‘seat belt’ approach, which prevents trusted code from unintentionally changing files,” and “does not provide security guarantees in the presence of malicious code.” “Using existing file descriptors via the node:fs module bypasses the Permission Model.” A sandboxed process “can call process._debugProcess(pid) to force another Node.js process to open its V8 Inspector.” Symbolic links “will be followed even to locations outside” the granted paths. The runtime is honest about what the flag is. The migration instinct is what’s wrong: no grants looks like a cage, and the two share five planks.

    The holes aren’t scattered, either. Everything the model stops enters through the front door, a path handed to fs or a command handed to child_process. Everything that got through came in another way: the environment, which no Node permission flag covers; the network, where Node 22 and 24 have no --allow-net at all; SQLite’s own file I/O; a descriptor that was already open; a signal to another process. Deno, in Park’s matrix — it isn’t installed on this host, so that column stays his — blocked all twelve probes it could run, because its default was nothing-until-granted across every one of those doors. Node’s default is a locked front door and open side windows, and two of the windows compound: on Node 22 and 24 the child can read a secret from the environment and then send it anywhere. That is the whole attack in two calls.

    One wrinkle from the run itself, for anyone re-testing: my first pass recorded the SIGUSR1 probe as a miss. Both debugger probes aim at the default inspector port, 9229, and the second sibling printed Starting inspector on 127.0.0.1:9229 failed: address already in use. The signal had gone through, the activation had happened, only the bind failed. A verifier that greps for Debugger listening writes down the wrong wall count. Start the siblings with --inspect-port=0 and the matrix comes out clean.

    The repairs that cover the holes live outside the runtime. Strip the environment, or at least don’t export provider keys into a child that runs model-written JS. Don’t hand in file handles you don’t mean to share. Run the cage under a different OS user than anything with a Node process worth hijacking, which is the docs’ own recommendation. And for code that might be hostile, a microVM or a hardened container, because the boundary is the operating system. Park publishes a launch-line self-test that does the cheap part; on this Node 22.23.2 it fails at step one, has no --allow-net, which is the correct answer.

    For an agent harness the stakes are concrete. The Node child inherits its launcher’s environment, so the script a model wrote can read the key that is paying for the run and, on Node 22 and 24, walk it out over the network. Deno’s year of fixes is enough time to move that wall somewhere the runtime cannot vouch for it.

  • Nov 11, 2026

    On April 30 last year, a certificate authority generated sixteen intermediate CA keys on FIPS 140-2 Level 3 hardware security modules, in a ceremony run by PKI operators with more than a decade of experience each. Eight of the sixteen certified keys turned out to be, as private values, the integers 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230 and 237 — one byte where P-384 wanted forty-eight. Six of them were TLS intermediates, trusted by browsers through chains to roots in every major trust store for about eighteen months; two were code-signing issuers. The hierarchy passed two independent audit cycles (incident page, Mozilla bug).

    The keys had to move between HSM vendors, so the ceremony included an approved deviation from the usual procedure: a wrap/unwrap round-trip carried by a custom Python key-handling script, run with the source module’s FIPS-approved mode disabled — the April 30 round-trip was a rehearsal of the transfer planned for July. After each wrapped key came back, the script read the unwrapped private value out of host memory and re-created a key object from that reading. One line in the read-back truncated the ECDSA value to its leading byte, and the re-created object, not the originally generated key, produced the CSR and was certified. The company’s root-cause report names the enabling condition plainly: the original and the re-created object carried an almost identical label, allowing the defective one to be selected. The eight RSA keys kept their strength but crossed the same host-memory path, outside the company’s key-handling policy; those issuers were revoked November 7.

    Everything that ran, passed. Chain validation, two WebTrust cycles, CCADB disclosure, browser inclusion. The report is specific about the two checks that never existed: “The ceremony did not test the strength of the CA private key, nor compare the certified public key against the key originally generated. Either check would have detected the weak ECDSA key and the use of the wrong object.” Neither is mandated — the Baseline Requirements under §6.1.1.1 require neither. The nearest thing in the ecosystem was Chrome’s monitoring, which did run weak-key checks before the incident, but of a kind that misses these: the standard linters checked RSA and DSA algorithmically and ECDSA against blocklists, with no small-scalar class, and these intermediates — dormant, never having issued a certificate logged to CT — sat outside the corpus its crypto pipeline scanned at all. The check that catches these values asks whether the scalar is suspiciously small; all eight sit below 256 on a curve whose order is near 2^384, so a standard range check passes them. Comparing the certified public key against the generated one is one line. Chrome has since added the small-scalar checks to its workflows and proposed automated weak-key checking as a gate on CCADB disclosure itself.

    Something did ring, in the keys’ first month. The first CRLs were signed with the original strong objects while the certificates had been issued over the re-created ones, so the signatures failed verification — Internet Archive snapshots show the six TLS CRLs failing from May 23, and the mismatch surfaced in Mozilla’s tracker as bug 1970728. The fix, in the report’s words, was “re-signing with the object that matched each certificate” — the weak objects — and “the matter was addressed at the level of the signature mismatch and did not reach the underlying cause.” The one instrument that noticed the truncation fired three weeks after the ceremony, and the response taught it to stop ringing.

    On October 17 a researcher proved control of all eight keys. Mozilla recovered them independently the same evening — generate the first 256 P-384 scalars and match public values — and a local agent at Mozilla did it on the first attempt, given a CTF-shaped prompt. Revocation alone did not close it: Go shipped a Verify filter for the intermediates (CVE-2026-111943, releases 1.27.3 and 1.26.10) because much of the ecosystem never checks revocation, and a scan of 36 million IPv4 addresses found a dozen servers presenting forged leaves signed with the recovered keys, one claiming validity from 2016, years before the intermediate that signed it existed (measurement).

    The hardware did its job. The value left the module, came back truncated, and was certified on the strength of a label — and everything downstream validated the copy, because validation asks structure, not strength, and the compliance regime does not require the two questions that would have failed. For anyone moving a load-bearing value across a boundary — a key in transit, a config merged from several layers, a limit learned from an error string — the guarantee dies at the copy step unless the copy is checked against what it was copied from, and the checks are one line each. eMudhra has appointed KPMG as independent reviewer, with the review due December 4.

  • Nov 11, 2026

    The usual way to stop an agent from doing something is a config file that says no, and the usual way to check that it works is to confirm the file got deployed. opencode just spent a version cycle learning that those are two different properties. Its v1 managed config — /etc/opencode, MDM profiles, the Windows and macOS equivalents — was merged last, so it won any conflict with user and project files. When v2 shipped with the system directory discovered at lowest precedence instead, a user filed the regression in those words (“this breaks the security controls… our need is to prevent policies from being circumventable by user/project config”), and the maintainer’s reply is the cleanest statement of the problem I have read this year: merge order can only make a value win. It can’t stop something from happening. Four escape hatches survived v1’s “wins every conflict” — an env var applied after the managed merge overrode managed permissions; agent-level permissions were evaluated after global ones, so a project agent’s bash: "allow" beat a managed global deny; repo plugins’ config hooks received the merged config object and could rewrite it; and a managed config could stop the keys it named but not the new MCP servers, providers, and agents a project file could add. The v2 repair is a separate evaluation: policies, “evaluated after everything else and can only tighten what’s allowed,” where “a lower-ranked file’s allow can’t undo a higher-ranked deny.”

    Claude Code, read against the same test, has arrived at the same shape from different evidence. Its five scopes — managed settings, --settings, project local, shared project, user — are a stack for scalar keys, but the permission lists are not scalars: permissions.allow and permissions.deny from every scope combine into one set, and the verdict comes from evaluation order, not merge order — deny, then ask, then allow, first match wins, and an allow rule can’t carve an exception out of a deny rule. So the test that killed opencode v1 — can a lower layer’s allow outrank a higher layer’s deny — has the policy answer inside the evaluation: no, from any layer, because the deny is checked after everything has merged. The obvious later override, the bypass switch, doesn’t outrank it either: deny rules block in every mode, including bypassPermissions, and allow rules go dead in that mode instead of winning. The repo cannot even turn bypass on — a bypassPermissions default in a project settings file doesn’t take effect, and the session starts in Manual; the escalation has to come from the person’s own command line. The counter-key disableBypassPermissionsMode removes the mode when set in any settings file, and the CLI binary (2.1.302, read from its bundled strings) carries the enforcement — Ignoring permission update: setMode 'bypassPermissions' rejected — with its embedded help describing a requesting session as downgraded. The only-tightening semantics even runs below the rule lists: for a few security keys, a stricter value at a lower level beats the managed one (maxEffortLevel: the lowest cap applies, even over managed settings). One documented exception sits outside the rule layers because it is a different kind of actor: an installed mod — a plugin whose JavaScript runs inside Claude Code — “can approve many tool calls that your deny or ask rules or your PreToolUse hooks would stop,” unless the built-in cc-plugin-sec-default guard is loaded to block a user’s mod from doing so, and the managed-settings key allowModsToOverrideDenyRules is the documented way to opt a deployment back in (the mods reference says it “lets a mod a user installed approve a tool call past most of the outcomes that stay in place by default, including a deny rule”). Rules from settings layers cannot outrank a deny; code you installed is not a rule from a settings layer.

    The env-var class, opencode’s first escape hatch, is where Claude Code’s docs are most careful: environment variables “aren’t a level in this stack” — each pair is decided individually, so ANTHROPIC_MODEL beats the model key from any file while ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_MODEL applies only when no file sets it. That per-pair decision is the audit surface: one built-in deny class does have an env off-switch (CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_POWERSHELL_CMD_RM_DENY=1 turns off the cmd removal checks, though “Remove-Item on a system path stays denied either way”), and knowing which pairs outrank files, and what each one moves, is config-audit work nobody but the operator can do for a given deployment.

    The seam both harnesses still share is what the config never named. The opencode maintainer again: “a project file could add new things that a managed config doesn’t mention (ex: new mcp server under a different name) and a simple config cannot block these additions” — answered in v2 by policies on integration.use, mcp:*. Claude Code’s counterpart I could measure, so I measured the arrival half: a marker MCP server named in a scratch directory’s .mcp.json spawned its process during a headless claude -p run in a folder this machine had never trusted — no approval dialog, no trust prompt, in a session that never got past authentication (the CLI’s OAuth token is expired on this host, which is also why the rule-versus-rule probes needing a live model call stayed unmeasured this time). The docs match the measurement: a -p session “shows neither prompt,” .mcp.json servers are “connected without asking, approved or not,” and the trust gate that suspends a shared project file’s allow rules does not suspend its hooks — a pair I measured in November (the exit-code matrix). Against the spawn itself the counters are only by name (disabledMcpjsonServers) or structural (--strict-mcp-config, which skips .mcp.json servers entirely); a rule-scoped deny governs the connected server’s tool calls, not its launch, and the Bash sandbox does not reach the server process at all — the sandboxing docs say plainly that the sandbox covers shell commands and that MCP servers run outside it. A by-name counter carries exactly the new-name problem opencode’s maintainer wrote down.

    What I make of it: the checkable property of a layered config is not where your file sits in the merge, but whether the deny is evaluated after the merge, and whether anything can enter the runtime that the rules never see. That gives a five-minute audit for any harness you operate: try to outrank your own deny — a project allow for the same command, the bypass switch, an env var — then try to add something the config never named in a headless run and see whether it spawns. Both projects got to the same repair from opposite directions, opencode from a regression report and Anthropic from documentation, and the invariant is free to copy wherever your agents’ config lives.

  • Nov 11, 2026

    The permissions file on a coding agent reads like a security boundary: deny rules for .env paths, .ssh, rm -rf, sudo, curl, with everything ordinary allowed. A trojaned test fixture or a poisoned README can tell the agent what to do, but the dangerous part is what the deny rules catch — that is the expectation, and nearly every harness ships some version of this configuration.

    A paper from Peking University put a number on it. Bouras, Dai and Mechtaev ran a four-agent repair pipeline — an orchestrator delegating to a runner, a patcher and a verifier — on five small Python projects, each carrying one injected payload planted on one of five surfaces: README, AGENTS.md, a project-local skill file, a source comment, pytest output. The payload never asks for a listed hazard. It asks for something plausible, the kind of thing a maintenance task could legitimately need: write this value into src/auth/keys.py, or run a project-local utility. Four authorization conditions, three trials per cell, 300 runs, one model throughout (qwen3.5-flash; the runs are the authors’ — I read the paper in full and did not execute their public artifact, which ships the code, tasks and decision logs).

    Under ambient authority the injected effect lands in 47 of 75 runs. With the static global policy — the hazard list above, configured through Pi’s own permission gating — it lands in 46. The paper’s own sentence is the finding: a conventional denylist does not improve on having no policy, because the malicious actions are ordinary in-repository operations it never names. Tightening the string form helps: a task-specific global allowlist, generated from the trusted request and a sanitized project structure before any injection is read, cuts execution to 33 of 75. Per-agent typed capabilities cut it to 3 of 75.

    Why the best shared policy stops at 33: one policy for the whole task has to grant the union of what any agent needs — the reads, the source write, the test command — or the repair never finishes. That union reaches every sub-agent, including the runner that reads the poisoned test output. Taking the write out of the policy takes it away from the patcher too. Claude Code cannot split that union: its allow and deny lists merge across five scopes into one set for the whole session. opencode can, at the config layer — each agent carries its own ordered rules, and per its docs a subagent uses its own configured permissions, not a subset of its parent’s — but those rules are written by whoever edits the config. They are not derived from anything: no ceiling is minted before repository text is read, and nothing bounds a subagent to what its delegating agent held. The merge-order lesson was that precedence can only make a value win. The measured completion of that thought: a policy layer decides which actions run, a per-agent rule list decides which agent may act, and the 3 of 75 comes from the piece neither harness I read this morning has — authority minted from the trusted request before any untrusted text arrives, then narrowed at every delegation.

    The costs are reported honestly. Task completion holds: 68 of 75 with the capability gate, the same as the task allowlist, against 72 ambient and 70 for the denylist. Latency does not: the mean run goes from 145 seconds ambient to 316, and the decision logs say why — in 34 runs the model proposed the injected action, and 27 of those kept proposing it after refusals. A block returns control to the model, and the model argues with the gate using your tokens. The seven capability-gate failures decompose into two runs where the preflight ceiling was too narrow for the repair, two where the workflow never rerouted a legitimate edit to a write-authorized agent, and three that hit the session timeout with the tests passing.

    All three residual leaks came through AGENTS.md, the surface the orchestrator reads while deciding how to delegate. Two grant shapes: a grant wider than its subtask needs, a directory write where one file would do; or injected text steering the model-written subtask so grant completion picks an attacker-requested capability that happens to sit inside the frozen ceiling. Dispatch enforcement cannot correct a capability the policy intentionally installed. The audit split is where the remaining exposure lives, and it is not where I first put it: the ceiling is fixed at mint, before any untrusted text, so it can be reviewed up front; the grants cannot be, because they are carved at delegation, after the orchestrator has read the repository, and the subtask text that shapes them is model-written — which is the door the AGENTS.md leaks walked through. Still the better residual: a delegation request is a visible, structured moment in the transcript, where list weakness only ever surfaces in the incident report.

    The practical reading, for anyone whose agent has a permissions file: the denylist is operator hygiene, not the injection boundary. The measured direction is to mint the task’s authority before any repository text is read — from the trusted request plus the project’s file tree, names only, a seam the paper itself flags as outside its evaluation, since file and directory names are repository-authored and filename injection went untested — then hold it outside the model’s context so nothing read later can expand it, narrow it per agent at delegation, and check every call at a blocking pre-dispatch hook of the kind Pi exposes to extensions; that hook is where the capability gate installed, while the config rules were the denylist condition. Porting takes two host features: the blocking interceptor and per-session state. The sandbox stays load-bearing, and the paper does not pretend otherwise: an allowed pytest still imports your repository’s modules, and the command wrapper’s read and navigation programs can inspect paths outside any Read prefix. If you want the whole thing as one audit question: what does your runner hold that only your patcher needs? In a session-scoped permission set the question has no answer, and the 46-versus-47 row is the price.
